question: Tell me about a time you noticed the visible, career-making work going to the same people.

raiseTranscript.text: On my team the same two engineers kept getting the customer-facing demos and the high-visibility features. I tracked the last four assignments and saw the pattern. I brought the list to my manager in our 1:1 and asked if we could rotate the next one to someone newer.
What happened after you raised it?
She agreed and we gave the next demo to a teammate who had never done one. He did well and now gets considered more often.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you noticed the visible, career-making work going to the same people.
Role: new engineer on 8-person team
Situation: noticed same two people always picked for demos and big features
Action: logged four assignments, raised in 1:1 with manager, suggested rotation
Outcome: next demo given to teammate who had never done one; pattern started to shift
Quote: "I brought the list to my manager and asked if we could rotate the next one."
Follow-up: What happened after you raised it? - Manager agreed and change stuck
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Diversity, Inclusion & Belonging for the question about noticing visible work going to the same people. The candidate tracked assignments on their own team and raised the pattern directly with their manager using a simple list. The quote shows they focused on a concrete, local fix rather than waiting for someone else. This produced an immediate rotation that benefited a teammate. The story stays within individual scope, which is appropriate for junior level. Biggest strength is the willingness to surface the issue with data instead of staying silent.

lowerTranscript.text: I saw that the same senior people always got the good projects but I figured that was just how it worked so I didn't say anything.
Did you ever mention it to anyone?
No, I just kept my head down and waited for my turn.

raiseTranscript.text: Across two product teams the same four engineers were always chosen for the launch demos and the customer escalations that led to promotions. I pulled assignment data for the prior two quarters and shared it with the two tech leads plus the TPM.

They agreed the data showed concentration. We set up a lightweight rotation process and tracked it for the next quarter; three additional people got visible work and one was promoted six months later.

Did you try to involve the other team?
No, I figured it was their call and didn't push further.

raiseTranscript.text: I saw that promotion and visibility opportunities were heavily concentrated among a small set of teams. I commissioned an org-wide review of project assignments and promotion cases over 18 months and found clear skews by team and tenure.
What did you do with the findings?

I presented the data to the leadership team and we changed the promotion calibration process to require explicit review of underrepresented teams. We also created a central visibility program; over the next year the share of promotions from previously overlooked teams rose from 12 percent to 29 percent.
